subject: science
passage: The tuatara of New Zealand looks much like a lizard, with its scaly body and long tail. It is not a lizard, however. It is the only surviving member of a group of reptiles that split from the ancestors of lizards and snakes more than two hundred million years ago, and it keeps features that no lizard has. Its teeth are not separate structures but sharp projections of the jawbone itself, and two rows in the upper jaw close over a single row in the lower. It also grows slowly and lives long: a tuatara may still be growing at thirty and can live for more than a century.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The tuatara survives in New Zealand because it has no competitors among lizards and snakes.
choices.B: The tuatara grows more slowly and lives longer than any other reptile.
choices.C: Although the tuatara resembles a lizard, it belongs to a separate, ancient line of reptiles.
choices.D: The tuatara's teeth are projections of its jawbone rather than separate structures.

explanation.why: The text first notes that the tuatara looks like a lizard, then states firmly that "it is not a lizard" and explains that it belongs to a very old group that split from lizards and snakes long ago. The details about its teeth, growth, and lifespan support that it is different from lizards.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text does not discuss competition or explain why the tuatara survives.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the tuatara grows slowly and lives long, but it does not compare it with every other reptile.
explanation.C: Correct. This captures the text's contrast between the tuatara's lizard-like appearance and its separate, ancient lineage.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The teeth are one supporting detail, not the main idea of the whole text.
